lesson.title: Every Average Imaginable: The Sampling Distribution of x-bar
lesson.summary: The sampling distribution of the mean describes how the value of x-bar would vary across every possible sample of a given size drawn from the population.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed that different samples produce different values of x-bar. The sampling distribution of x-bar is the distribution formed by every possible value of x-bar across every sample of size n that could be drawn, weighted by how likely each sample is. It plays exactly the same role for the sample mean that the sampling distribution of p-hat played for the sample proportion.

A small enumerated example again makes this concrete. Consider a tiny population of four values: 2, 4, 6, and 8. The population mean is mu = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8) / 4 = 20 / 4 = 5. Suppose we draw a simple random sample of two values without replacement and compute x-bar each time. There are exactly six possible samples of size two from these four values: {2,4}, {2,6}, {2,8}, {4,6}, {4,8}, and {6,8}.

Computing the sample mean for each: {2,4} gives x-bar = 3, {2,6} gives x-bar = 4, {2,8} gives x-bar = 5, {4,6} gives x-bar = 5, {4,8} gives x-bar = 6, and {6,8} gives x-bar = 7. Notice that x-bar = 5 shows up twice, from two different samples, while the other values each show up once. Collecting this into a table, the sampling distribution of x-bar assigns probability 1/6 to each of 3, 4, 6, and 7, and probability 2/6 to the value 5.

Even in this tiny example with only six possible samples, a pattern is visible that will become important later: the values cluster more heavily near the center, 5, than at the extremes, 3 and 7. With a real population and larger samples, this clustering toward the center becomes far more pronounced, and it is one of the threads that leads to the Central Limit Theorem later in this unit. For now, the key idea is the same as with proportions: the sampling distribution of x-bar is a full distribution of possible sample means, not a single number, and the next two chapters describe its center and its spread precisely.
